notes.front: What is the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR)?
notes.back: Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR): the IRS office with exclusive delegated authority and oversight over tax practitioner conduct and discipline.
notes.explanation: It investigates and disciplines violations of Circular 230, including by instituting disciplinary proceedings.
notes.example: Like a professional regulator’s disciplinary board, but for people who practise before the IRS.
notes.source: Office of Professional Responsibility and Circular 230 (IRS.gov)
notes.evidence: The OPR has exclusive delegated authority and oversight responsibility for tax practitioner conduct and discipline.

notes.front: Under the Code’s penalty for frivolous tax submissions, what makes a submission frivolous?
notes.back: It is based on a position the IRS has identified as frivolous, or it reflects a desire to delay or impede tax administration.
notes.explanation: The IRS must publish, and periodically revise, its list of positions identified as frivolous.
notes.example: Like a hearing request filed only to stall a levy.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6702 (Internal Revenue Code), “(b) Civil penalty for specified frivolous submissions”
notes.evidence: (i) is based on a position which the Secretary has identified as frivolous under subsection (c), or (ii) reflects a desire to delay or impede the administration of Federal tax laws.

notes.front: What are badges of fraud?
notes.back: Signs of possible fraud, which the IRS fraud handbook also calls first indicators of fraud.
notes.explanation: The handbook says fraud itself is substantiated by establishing affirmative acts of fraud.
notes.example: Like warning lights on a dashboard: they signal something may be wrong without proving it.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.2, Recognizing and Developing Fraud, “25.1.2.1.1 Background”
notes.evidence: This section discusses recognizing signs of fraud, known as first indicators (or badges) of fraud, and the development process used to prove fraud.

notes.front: What is tax avoidance, as the IRS fraud handbook describes it?
notes.back: Reducing, avoiding or minimising tax by legitimate means; it is not a criminal offence.
notes.explanation: One who avoids tax does not conceal or misrepresent, but shapes and plans events within the law.
notes.example: Like timing a share sale into a later year to fall in a lower bracket, openly and within the rules.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.1, Fraud Handbook: Overview/Definitions, “25.1.1.3.3 Avoidance vs. Evasion”
notes.evidence: Avoidance of tax is not a criminal offense. Taxpayers have the right to reduce, avoid, or minimize their taxes by legitimate means.

notes.front: What is tax evasion, as the IRS fraud handbook describes it?
notes.back: An affirmative act to evade or defeat a tax or its payment, such as deceit, concealment or making things seem other than they are.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives deceit, subterfuge, camouflage and concealment as examples of affirmative acts.
notes.example: Like disguising a family holiday as a business trip to deduct it.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.1, Fraud Handbook: Overview/Definitions, “25.1.1.3.3 Avoidance vs. Evasion”
notes.evidence: Evasion involves some affirmative act to evade or defeat a tax, or payment of tax. Examples of affirmative acts are deceit, subterfuge, camouflage, concealment, attempts to color or obscure events, or make things seem other than they are.

notes.front: Under Circular 230, who is a tax return preparer?
notes.back: Any individual within the meaning of Code section 7701(a)(36) and Treasury Regulation 301.7701-15.
notes.explanation: Those regulations set the rules on who is a signing and who a nonsigning tax return preparer.
notes.example: Like the paid preparer whose name and PTIN appear on a client’s return.
notes.source: 31 CFR Part 10 (Treasury Department Circular No. 230), 1 July 2025 edition, “§ 10.2 Definitions”, p. 3

notes.front: Under section 6694(a), when is a return position an unreasonable position?
notes.back: Generally, unless there is or was substantial authority for it; a properly disclosed position needs only a reasonable basis.
notes.explanation: Tax shelter and reportable transaction positions must be reasonably believed more likely than not to be sustained.
notes.example: Like an undisclosed claim with no ruling, regulation or other authority behind it.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6694 (Internal Revenue Code), “(a)(2) Unreasonable position”
notes.evidence: Except as otherwise provided in this paragraph, a position is described in this paragraph unless there is or was substantial authority for the position.

notes.front: Under section 6694(b), what is willful or reckless conduct by a tax return preparer?
notes.back: A wilful attempt in any manner to understate the tax liability, or a reckless or intentional disregard of rules or regulations.
notes.explanation: Either kind of conduct triggers the higher section 6694(b) penalty.
notes.example: Like a preparer inventing charitable gifts to shrink a client’s tax bill.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6694 (Internal Revenue Code), “(b)(2) Willful or reckless conduct”
notes.evidence: (A) a willful attempt in any manner to understate the liability for tax on the return or claim, or (B) a reckless or intentional disregard of rules or regulations.

notes.front: What is the accuracy-related penalty?
notes.back: An addition to tax of 20% of the portion of an underpayment to which section 6662 applies.
notes.explanation: Section 6662 applies to portions due to causes such as negligence or a substantial understatement of income tax.
notes.example: Like a 20% surcharge on the part of the tax that was underpaid through carelessness.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(a) Imposition of penalty”
notes.evidence: there shall be added to the tax an amount equal to 20 percent of the portion of the underpayment to which this section applies.

notes.front: In section 6662, what does negligence include?
notes.back: Any failure to make a reasonable attempt to comply with the Internal Revenue Code.
notes.explanation: Negligence or disregard of rules or regulations is the first ground listed for the accuracy-related penalty.
notes.example: Like not bothering to check whether a large deduction is allowed at all.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(c) Negligence”
notes.evidence: the term "negligence" includes any failure to make a reasonable attempt to comply with the provisions of this title

notes.front: For an individual, when is there a substantial understatement of income tax?
notes.back: When the understatement exceeds the greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown or $5,000.
notes.explanation: Corporations other than S corporations and personal holding companies have their own test. Figures from 26 U.S.C. § 6662 as read in 2026; its 2025 amendment added only subsection (m), so they applied throughout 2025.
notes.example: Like a two-part hurdle: the understatement must clear both 10% of the correct tax and $5,000.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(d) Substantial understatement of income tax”
notes.evidence: there is a substantial understatement of income tax for any taxable year if the amount of the understatement for the taxable year exceeds the greater of- (i) 10 percent of the tax required to be shown on the return for the taxable year, or (ii) $5,000.

notes.front: What is a substantial valuation misstatement under chapter 1?
notes.back: Claiming a property’s value or adjusted basis at 150% or more of the correct amount.
notes.explanation: It also covers certain transfer-pricing misstatements between related parties under section 482.
notes.example: Like claiming a donated painting worth $10,000 at $16,000.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(e) Substantial valuation misstatement under chapter 1”
notes.evidence: the value of any property (or the adjusted basis of any property) claimed on any return of tax imposed by chapter 1 is 150 percent or more of the amount determined to be the correct amount of such valuation or adjusted basis

notes.front: What is a gross valuation misstatement?
notes.back: A valuation misstatement past higher thresholds; for a property’s value or basis, 200% or more of the correct amount instead of 150%.
notes.explanation: For the portion of the underpayment it causes, the penalty rate doubles from 20% to 40%.
notes.example: Like claiming $25,000 for an asset worth $10,000.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(h) Increase in penalty in case of gross valuation misstatements”
notes.evidence: The term "gross valuation misstatements" means- (A) any substantial valuation misstatement under chapter 1 as determined under subsection (e) by substituting- (i) in paragraph (1)(A), "200 percent" for "150 percent"

notes.front: What is the civil fraud penalty?
notes.back: An addition to tax of 75% of the portion of an underpayment attributable to fraud.
notes.explanation: The accuracy-related penalty does not apply to any portion on which the fraud penalty is imposed.
notes.example: Like the 20% accuracy-related penalty’s far heavier counterpart, for underpayments caused by fraud.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6663 (Internal Revenue Code), “(a) Imposition of penalty”
notes.evidence: If any part of any underpayment of tax required to be shown on a return is due to fraud, there shall be added to the tax an amount equal to 75 percent of the portion of the underpayment which is attributable to fraud.

notes.front: Distributing profits to fictitious partners belongs to which category of fraud indicators in the IRS fraud handbook?
notes.back: Allocations of income.
notes.explanation: Shifting income or deductions to a related taxpayer where tax rates differ is in the same category.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.2, Recognizing and Developing Fraud, “25.1.2.3 Indicators of Fraud”
notes.evidence: Distribution of profits to fictitious partners.

notes.front: Destroying books and records just after an examination starts belongs to which category of fraud indicators in the IRS fraud handbook?
notes.back: Conduct of taxpayer.
notes.explanation: Attempts to hinder the examination, and failing to follow a preparer’s advice, are in the same category.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.2, Recognizing and Developing Fraud, “25.1.2.3 Indicators of Fraud”
notes.evidence: Destruction of books and records, especially if just after examination was started.

notes.front: Placing ownership of assets in other people’s names belongs to which category of fraud indicators in the IRS fraud handbook?
notes.back: Methods of concealment.
notes.explanation: Transfers for inadequate consideration, or between closely related parties, are in the same category.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.2, Recognizing and Developing Fraud, “25.1.2.3 Indicators of Fraud”
notes.evidence: Asset ownership placed in other names.

notes.front: Which of these is tax avoidance rather than tax evasion?
notes.back: A: Openly timing a planned asset sale into a lower-tax year.
notes.choices:
A) Openly timing a planned asset sale into a lower-tax year
B) Keeping cash takings out of the business account and off the return
C) Back-dating invoices to move income into a later year
notes.choicesExplained: B and C involve concealment or making things seem other than they are, which are affirmative acts of evasion.
notes.explanation: Avoidance shapes and plans events within the law without concealing or misrepresenting.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.1, Fraud Handbook: Overview/Definitions, “25.1.1.3.3 Avoidance vs. Evasion”
notes.evidence: One who avoids tax does not conceal or misrepresent, but shapes and preplans events to reduce or eliminate tax liability within the parameters of the law.

notes.front: A preparer charged $3,000 for a return with an undisclosed position lacking substantial authority, which she should have known of. There is no reasonable cause. What is the section 6694(a) penalty?
notes.choicesExplained: B is the floor, used only when 50% of the income is lower. C applies the 75% rate of section 6694(b).
notes.explanation: 50% of $3,000 is $1,500, which is greater than $1,000. Amount from 26 U.S.C. § 6694 as read in 2026; last amended in 2015, so in force throughout 2025.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6694 (Internal Revenue Code), “(a)(1) In general”
notes.evidence: in an amount equal to the greater of $1,000 or 50 percent of the income derived (or to be derived) by the tax return preparer with respect to the return or claim.

notes.front: A preparer deliberately inflated a client’s deductions and charged a $2,000 fee. What is the section 6694(b) penalty?
notes.choicesExplained: B is 75% of the fee, which is lower than $5,000. C is the section 6694(a) floor.
notes.explanation: A wilful attempt to understate the liability is willful or reckless conduct. Amount from 26 U.S.C. § 6694 as read in 2026; last amended in 2015, so in force throughout 2025.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6694 (Internal Revenue Code), “(b)(1) In general”
notes.evidence: in an amount equal to the greater of- (A) $5,000, or (B) 75 percent of the income derived (or to be derived) by the tax return preparer with respect to the return or claim.

notes.front: A preparer receives notice and demand for a $5,000 section 6694(b) penalty that she disputes. What must she do within 30 days to hold off collection?
notes.back: Pay at least $750 (15%) and file a claim for refund of that amount.
notes.explanation: She must then sue in district court within 30 days of any denial of the claim.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6694 (Internal Revenue Code), “(c) Extension of period of collection where preparer pays 15 percent of penalty”
notes.evidence: such person pays an amount which is not less than 15 percent of the amount of such penalty and files a claim for refund of the amount so paid

notes.front: Without reasonable cause, a preparer gives clients no copies of their returns and leaves her identifying number off them. Which section 6695 penalties apply?
notes.back: Section 6695(a), for not furnishing copies, and section 6695(c), for not furnishing her identifying number, for each failure.
notes.explanation: Sections 6107(a) and 6109(a)(4) set the underlying duties.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6695 (Internal Revenue Code), “(a) and (c)”
notes.evidence: Any person who is a tax return preparer with respect to any return or claim for refund and who fails to comply with section 6109(a)(4) with respect to such return or claim shall pay a penalty of $50 for such failure

notes.front: A preparer endorses three clients’ refund cheques and cashes them through an agent. What does section 6695(f) impose?
notes.back: Three penalties, one per cheque: $1,500 at the $500 statutory base, which is indexed for inflation.
notes.explanation: Negotiating “directly or through an agent” is covered. Base from 26 U.S.C. § 6695 as read in 2026; § 6695(h) indexes it, so the 2025 figure differs.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6695 (Internal Revenue Code), “(f) Negotiation of check”
notes.evidence: Any person who is a tax return preparer who endorses or otherwise negotiates (directly or through an agent) any check made in respect of the taxes imposed by this title which is issued to a taxpayer (other than the tax return preparer) shall pay a penalty of $500 with respect to each such check.

notes.front: A client claims head of household and the EIC. The preparer fills in Form 8867 but never asks where the child lived and keeps no notes. Has she met the due diligence requirements?
notes.back: No. The knowledge requirement needs adequate questions with the answers documented at the time.
notes.explanation: Failure to meet the due diligence requirements can bring a penalty for each failure.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8867 (Rev. November 2025), “General Instructions”, p. 2
notes.evidence: diligence requirements could result in a penalty for each failure.

notes.front: On one return filed in 2026, a preparer fails the due diligence requirements for both the EIC and the AOTC. Using the Form 8867 instructions’ figure, what penalty could apply?
notes.back: $1,300: $650 for each of the two failures.
notes.explanation: The penalty applies to each failure, so two failed benefits mean two penalties. The $650 figure is for returns filed in 2026; the exam uses 2025 amounts, which may differ.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8867 (Rev. November 2025), “Consequences of Not Meeting Your Due Diligence Requirements”, p. 4
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Form 8867 instructions Rev. November 2025 (returns filed in 2026)
notes.evidence: $650 for each of the four credits claimed for a tax return filed in

notes.front: A paid preparer decides a client’s head of household status, but a colleague signs the return. What does the first preparer do with her Form 8867?
notes.back: As a nonsigning preparer, she gives the completed form, electronically or on paper, to the signing preparer.
notes.explanation: The signing preparer then files it with the return.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8867 (Rev. November 2025), “Nonsigning tax return preparers”, p. 1
notes.evidence: required to sign the return as preparer, provide the signing tax

notes.front: A preparer prepared a return during the return period that ended on 30 June 2026. Until when must she keep its copy or her client list?
notes.back: Until 30 June 2029: 3 years after the close of the return period.
notes.explanation: Section 6107(d) takes “return period” from section 6060(c): the 12 months beginning 1 July.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6107 (Internal Revenue Code), “(b) Copy or list to be retained by tax return preparer”
notes.evidence: for the period ending 3 years after the close of the return period

notes.front: Maya works alone as a paid preparer with no employer. Does section 6060 apply to her?
notes.back: Yes. A preparer who is not another preparer’s employee is treated as his or her own employer.
notes.explanation: The IRS may approve an alternative reporting method if it has the information from other sources.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6060 (Internal Revenue Code), “(a) General rule”
notes.evidence: any individual who in acting as a tax return preparer is not the employee of another tax return preparer shall be treated as his own employer.

notes.front: Through negligence, a taxpayer underpaid tax by $4,000. What accuracy-related penalty applies to that portion?
notes.back: $800: 20% of the $4,000 portion attributable to negligence.
notes.explanation: The penalty is figured on the portion of the underpayment to which section 6662 applies.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(a) Imposition of penalty”
notes.evidence: there shall be added to the tax an amount equal to 20 percent of the portion of the underpayment to which this section applies.

notes.front: An individual’s correct tax is $80,000, but her return shows $71,000, with no items reduced for authority or disclosure. Is there a substantial understatement?
notes.back: A: Yes; $9,000 exceeds the greater of $8,000 and $5,000.
notes.choices:
A) Yes; $9,000 exceeds the greater of $8,000 and $5,000
B) No; $9,000 is less than 10% of $80,000
C) No; only understatements over $10,000 count
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: 10% of $80,000 is $8,000, below $9,000. C is wrong: $10,000 is part of the corporate test, not the individual one.
notes.explanation: The test compares the understatement with the greater of 10% of the correct tax and $5,000. Figures from 26 U.S.C. § 6662 as read in 2026; its 2025 amendment added only subsection (m), so they applied throughout 2025.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(d) Substantial understatement of income tax”
notes.evidence: exceeds the greater of- (i) 10 percent of the tax required to be shown on the return for the taxable year, or (ii) $5,000.

notes.front: A taxpayer claims an adjusted basis of $180,000 for property whose correct basis is $100,000, causing a $12,000 underpayment. Which misstatement is this?
notes.back: A: A substantial valuation misstatement (20%).
notes.choices:
A) A substantial valuation misstatement (20%)
B) A gross valuation misstatement (40%)
C) No valuation misstatement
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: 180% is below the 200% gross threshold. C is wrong: 180% exceeds 150%, and the underpayment exceeds $5,000.
notes.explanation: The claimed basis is 180% of the correct amount. Figures from 26 U.S.C. § 6662 as read in 2026; its 2025 amendment added only subsection (m), so they applied throughout 2025.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(e) Substantial valuation misstatement under chapter 1”
notes.evidence: is 150 percent or more of the amount determined to be the correct amount of such valuation or adjusted basis (as the case may be)

notes.front: A taxpayer claims a value of $250,000 for property worth $100,000, and this causes a $30,000 underpayment. What penalty applies to that portion?
notes.back: $12,000: 40% of $30,000, because 250% is at least the 200% gross valuation threshold.
notes.explanation: Below 200% but at least 150%, the rate would be 20%.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(h) Increase in penalty in case of gross valuation misstatements”
notes.evidence: subsection (a) shall be applied with respect to such portion by substituting "40 percent" for "20 percent".

notes.front: The IRS proves fraud in part of a $20,000 underpayment. The taxpayer proves by a preponderance of the evidence that $4,000 of it was not due to fraud. What is the civil fraud penalty?
notes.choicesExplained: B is 75% of the whole $20,000, ignoring the portion she disproved. C is 20% of the whole underpayment.
notes.explanation: 75% of the remaining $16,000 is $12,000.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6663 (Internal Revenue Code), “(b) Determination of portion attributable to fraud”
notes.evidence: except with respect to any portion of the underpayment which the taxpayer establishes (by a preponderance of the evidence) is not attributable to fraud.

notes.front: Without authority, a preparer knowingly sells clients’ names and incomes to a marketing firm. Which Code provisions does this engage?
notes.back: Section 7216, a criminal misdemeanour, and section 6713, a civil penalty of $250 per disclosure up to $10,000 a year.
notes.explanation: Wilful unauthorised disclosure is also disreputable conduct under § 10.51(a)(15) for a practitioner. Amounts from 26 U.S.C. § 6713 as read in 2026; last amended in 2019, so in force throughout 2025.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7216 (Internal Revenue Code), “(a) General rule”
notes.evidence: and who knowingly or recklessly- (1) discloses any information furnished to him for, or in connection with, the preparation of any such return, or (2) uses any such information for any purpose other than to prepare, or assist in preparing, any such return

notes.front: Tax avoidance versus tax evasion: what separates them?
notes.back: Avoidance uses legitimate means and hides nothing; evasion involves an affirmative act such as deceit or concealment.
notes.explanation: The fraud handbook says avoidance is not a criminal offence.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.1, Fraud Handbook: Overview/Definitions, “25.1.1.3.3 Avoidance vs. Evasion”
notes.evidence: One who avoids tax does not conceal or misrepresent, but shapes and preplans events to reduce or eliminate tax liability within the parameters of the law.

notes.front: Civil versus criminal tax fraud: what must the government prove each by?
notes.back: Civil fraud: clear and convincing evidence. Criminal fraud: proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
notes.explanation: In both, the burden of proof is on the government.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.1, Fraud Handbook: Overview/Definitions, “25.1.1.3.1 Requirements of Proof”
notes.evidence: In criminal cases, the government must present sufficient evidence to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. In civil fraud cases, the government must prove fraud by clear and convincing evidence.

notes.front: Section 6694(a) versus section 6694(b): what triggers each, and how much is each?
notes.back: (a) an unreasonable position: greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income. (b) willful or reckless conduct: greater of $5,000 or 75%.
notes.explanation: Any (b) penalty is reduced by the (a) penalty paid on the same return. Amount from 26 U.S.C. § 6694 as read in 2026; last amended in 2015, so in force throughout 2025.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6694 (Internal Revenue Code), “(a) and (b)”
notes.evidence: in an amount equal to the greater of $1,000 or 50 percent of the income derived (or to be derived) by the tax return preparer with respect to the return or claim.

notes.front: Censure versus suspension: may the practitioner keep practising?
notes.back: Censure: yes, possibly under conditions. Suspension: no, not during the suspension period.
notes.explanation: Conditions may follow either sanction.
notes.source: 31 CFR Part 10 (Treasury Department Circular No. 230), 1 July 2025 edition, “§ 10.79 Effect of disbarment, suspension, or censure”, p. 38
notes.evidence: the sanction of either suspension or

notes.front: Circular 230 § 10.31 versus Code section 6695(f): how do they differ?
notes.back: § 10.31: a Circular 230 rule for practitioners, enforced by sanctions. Section 6695(f): a Code penalty on preparers for each cheque ($500 base, indexed).
notes.explanation: Both concern negotiating a client’s government tax cheque. Base from 26 U.S.C. § 6695 as read in 2026; § 6695(h) indexes it, so the 2025 figure differs.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6695 (Internal Revenue Code), “(f) Negotiation of check”
notes.evidence: shall pay a penalty of $500 with respect to each such check.

notes.front: Accuracy-related penalty versus civil fraud penalty: what rates apply, and can they overlap?
notes.back: 20% (40% for gross valuation misstatements) versus 75%; section 6662 does not apply to any portion on which the fraud penalty is imposed.
notes.explanation: The fraud penalty covers portions of the underpayment attributable to fraud.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (Internal Revenue Code), “(b) Portion of underpayment to which section applies”
notes.evidence: This section shall not apply to any portion of an underpayment on which a penalty is imposed under section 6663.
